questions.q: VAT is rounded down instead of to the nearest kobo. What is the cheapest test that catches this?
questions.explain: The rule lives in one pure function. A unit test with a carefully chosen boundary value catches it in milliseconds, with no server or database.
options: A unit test of the pricing function with a price whose VAT ends in half a kobo
An end-to-end test that places an order over HTTP
A load test
A contract test against the payment provider

questions.q: The SQL that saves an order writes the total into the subtotal column. Which test catches it?
questions.explain: A fake store has no SQL, so it cannot have this bug. Only running the real SQL against a real database (PGlite is enough) exercises it.
options: A unit test of the checkout service with an in-memory fake store
An integration test of the store against a real database
A property-based test of priceCart
A spy on the mailer

questions.q: All tests use a hand-written payment fake that takes naira; the real provider takes kobo. Which kind of test is designed to catch this?
questions.explain: The bug is a difference between the fake and reality. Only a test that runs the same expectations against both can see it.
options: More unit tests of the checkout service
A test with 100% line coverage
A contract test: one suite that runs against both the fake and the provider's sandbox
A load test against staging

questions.q: Customer B can read customer A's order by changing the id in the URL. What must a test do to catch it?
questions.explain: This is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference). A test with a single user can never see it; it needs two real users and an attempt to cross the line between them.
options: Log in as A and read A's order
Create an order as A, then ask for it as B and expect 404 (or 403)
Mock the database so it returns no orders
Measure the response time of the order route

questions.q: What is a dummy?
questions.explain: A dummy exists because a constructor or function needs something. Making it throw when used, as the lesson's mailer does, also proves that the path under test really does not use it.
options: A double that returns canned answers
A double that records its calls
An object passed only to fill a parameter, which the test path never uses
A simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory store

questions.q: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
questions.explain: A stub is about inputs to your code ("the card is declined"). A mock is about outputs of your code ("you must charge exactly this amount, once"). Libraries often call every double a mock, which is where the confusion comes from.
options: There is none; they are two names for the same thing
A stub is for classes, a mock is for functions
A stub gives canned answers so a path can run; a mock knows which calls it expects and fails when they do not happen
A mock is always faster than a stub

questions.q: A checkout must send exactly one receipt with the formatted total. Which double fits best?
questions.explain: The receipt is the observable effect. A spy records the call so the test can assert on the count and the arguments without sending mail.
options: A dummy mailer
A spy mailer that records calls, checked after the checkout
A stub gateway that declines
No double: send a real e-mail

questions.q: When is a fake (a working in-memory implementation) the right double?
questions.explain: A fake is written once and reused by many tests. It behaves like the real thing in a simple way. Because it is code with its own behaviour, it should be kept honest by a contract suite.
options: When a test must prove a method is never called
When many tests need realistic behaviour from a dependency, such as saving and finding orders
When you need to test the real SQL
Only in end-to-end tests

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against mocking your own pure code, such as priceCart?
questions.explain: Mock the edges you do not control (providers, mail, the clock, the network). Your own pure logic is fast and deterministic, so use the real thing.
options: Because mocks cannot replace pure functions
The test then checks that the code calls the mock as scripted, not that checkout works; it breaks on harmless refactors and misses real bugs
Because pure functions are too slow to call in tests
Because TypeScript forbids it

questions.q: What do builders like aLine({ quantity: 0 }) give you over copying object literals into every test?
questions.explain: The default lives in one function. The override states the test's intent. And because each call returns a new object, one test cannot change another test's fixture.
options: They make tests run faster
One place to update when the type changes, a test that shows only what it cares about, and a fresh object per call
They generate random data like fast-check
They replace the need for assertions

questions.q: A test passes in the full suite but fails when run alone. What is the most likely cause, and how can you find such tests on purpose?
questions.explain: Shared state (a module variable, database rows, the clock) makes results depend on order. A random order exposes it, and --test-random-seed lets you reproduce the exact order that failed.
options: The test runner is broken; run it again
It depends on state left by an earlier test; run the suite in random order (--test-randomize) with a seed to repeat a failing order
It is too fast; add a delay
It needs more assertions

questions.q: Each database test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back. Which assertion becomes unreliable?
questions.explain: Rows are rolled back, but sequences are not: serial ids keep counting across tests. Assert on data you control, not on generated ids.
options: That the table is empty at the start of a test
That a stored JSON value reads back equal
That a new order gets id 1
That a CHECK constraint refuses a bad value

questions.q: When can you not isolate a test by wrapping it in a transaction that is rolled back?
questions.explain: Other connections cannot see (or be rolled back by) the test's open transaction, and nested BEGINs do not work the way the code expects. Give those tests a fresh database instead.
options: When the test only reads data
When the code under test opens its own transactions or uses other connections
When the table has a primary key
When the test uses PGlite

questions.q: The end-to-end tests use a real database but a fake payment provider. Why is that a sensible boundary?
questions.explain: Calling a real sandbox on every commit makes the suite slow and flaky. The contract suite, run against the sandbox on a schedule, is what keeps the fake trustworthy.
options: Because payment providers do not have test modes
Your whole system is exercised, while the provider's behaviour is covered by contract tests that are slower and run separately
Because the fake makes the tests more realistic
Because databases cannot be faked

questions.q: How does the lesson run the payment gateway contract suite?
questions.explain: The fake run is fast and keeps your code honest against the contract. The sandbox run keeps the fake honest against reality. Without its settings, that suite is skipped with a reason instead of failing.
options: Only against the fake, on every commit
Only against the provider's sandbox, on every commit
Against the fake on every commit, and against the sandbox when its settings are present (for example nightly)
Only by hand, before a release

questions.q: What is consumer-driven contract testing?
questions.explain: The consumers state what they depend on, so the provider learns before a release whether a change would break one of them. Pact is a common tool for it.
options: The API team writes tests for every possible client
The client team records the requests it makes and the answers it relies on, and the API team runs those expectations in its own CI
Customers report bugs, which become tests
A load test driven by real customer traffic

questions.q: What does fast-check do when it shrinks a failing input?
questions.explain: A random failing cart may have five lines of huge prices. Shrinking turns it into something like "one free item and a 1 kobo voucher", which points straight at the bug.
options: It compresses the test output
It keeps simplifying the failing input while it still fails, and reports the smallest one it finds
It reduces the number of runs to save time
It removes the assertion that failed

questions.q: A property test failed in CI but passes on your laptop. What in fast-check's report helps you reproduce it?
questions.explain: fast-check's generator is pseudo-random. The same seed gives the same sequence of inputs, and the path jumps straight to the shrunk counterexample.
options: The number of runs
The seed (and path): passing them back generates the same inputs again
The test's duration
Nothing; random tests cannot be reproduced

questions.q: Which property is an oracle?
questions.explain: An oracle compares the real code with a simpler reference calculation. The others are an invariant, a symmetry and a round trip.
options: "The total is never negative"
"The order of the lines does not change the total"
"The VAT is within half a kobo of the exact 7.5% calculated the simple way"
"Decoding an encoded cursor gives back the id"

questions.q: Fuzzing found that the product code "toString" gets a "price". Why, and what is a correct fix?
questions.explain: CATALOG["toString"] finds an inherited method. Freezing does not change inheritance, and a type annotation changes nothing at runtime. A Map only contains the entries you put in it.
options: JavaScript converts every string key to a number; use parseInt
A plain object inherits toString from Object.prototype; look prices up in a Map (or check Object.hasOwn)
The catalog was not frozen; use Object.freeze
The type should be Record<string, number | undefined>; nothing else is needed

questions.q: Why does a load test report p95 and p99 latency instead of only the average?
questions.explain: If 95 requests take 20 ms and 5 take 3 seconds, the average looks fine while 1 in 20 customers waits 3 seconds. Budgets are usually stated as percentiles for this reason.
options: Percentiles are easier to compute
An average hides the slow tail; p95 and p99 show what the unluckiest customers experience
The average is always larger than p99
Percentiles include the error rate

questions.q: Where should the lesson's k6 checkout scenario run?
questions.explain: A load test is a controlled attack on your own system. Running it on production can take the shop down and create real charges. Staging with fakes gives useful numbers safely.
options: Against production during the busiest hour, to be realistic
Against a staging copy with a fake payment provider, with a plan and permission
On a developer's laptop against the real payment provider
Nowhere: load tests are not useful for APIs

questions.q: A test fails about once in twenty runs with no code change. What should the team do?
questions.explain: A suite people have learned to re-run teaches them to ignore red. Flakiness almost always comes from shared state, real time or the network, which are the same isolation problems the lesson covers.
options: Add an automatic retry so CI stays green
Ignore it; flaky tests are normal
Treat it as a bug: find the shared state, timing or network dependency and fix it, or delete the test
Run it only on Fridays

questions.q: What is the right way to use test coverage?
questions.explain: Coverage says which lines ran, not whether the assertions were meaningful. A test with no real assertions can cover every line.
options: Require 100% coverage and stop writing tests after that
Look for untested branches to decide what to test next; do not treat the number as proof of quality
Ignore it entirely
Use it instead of code review

questions.q: A hand-made table-driven test. What does it print?
questions.explain: 7.5% of 7 kobo is 0.525, and Math.round rounds it to 1, so the table row that expected 0 fails. The half-up row passes: 18,753.75 rounds to 18,754. Each row names its case, so a failure points straight at the boundary that misbehaves, and here it shows that the table itself held the wrong expectation.
options:
PASS whole: 75000
PASS half up: 18754
PASS tiny: 0

PASS whole: 75000
PASS half up: 18754
FAIL tiny: 1

PASS whole: 75000
FAIL half up: 18753
PASS tiny: 0

PASS whole: 75000
FAIL half up: 18753
FAIL tiny: 1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A spy records every call and its arguments. Only the two paid checkouts sent mail, so there are two calls; the first one's arguments are the customer id and the subject.
options: 2 undefined

questions.q: Two "tests" share one fixture object. What does this print?
questions.explain: const line = RICE copies the reference, not the object, so the bulk test changed the shared fixture. The same single-item test now gives a different answer depending on what ran before it. Builders that return a fresh object prevent this.
options:
single: 950000
bulk: 9500000
single: 950000

single: 950000
bulk: 9500000
single: 9500000

single: 9500000
bulk: 9500000
single: 9500000

single: 950000
bulk: 950000
single: 950000

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call builds a new object from the defaults plus the overrides. So a keeps quantity 1, b gets 3 and keeps the default SKU, and two calls never return the same object.
options: 3 3 RICE-5KG true
1 3 RICE-5KG true
1 3 RICE-5KG false
1 3 undefined false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: One slow request pulls the average up to 102.2 ms, although nine of ten took 16 ms or less. The percentiles tell the real story: the median is 14 ms, p90 is 16 ms, and the worst case is 900 ms.

questions.q: Two properties, checked with a fixed seed. What does this print?
questions.explain: Reversing twice is a true round-trip property. "Every array is already sorted" is false, and fast-check shrinks whatever random array it found first down to the smallest unsorted one: [1, 0].
options:
reverse twice holds
already sorted holds

reverse twice holds
already sorted fails: Counterexample: [[1,0]]

reverse twice holds
already sorted fails: Counterexample: [[9,3,7,1,0]]

reverse twice fails: Counterexample: [[1,0]]
already sorted fails: Counterexample: [[1,0]]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type says every key gives a number, but toString is inherited from Object.prototype. A Map has no inherited entries, and Object.hasOwn only sees the object's own keys.
options:
undefined true
undefined false

function false
undefined false

function false
function true

number false
undefined false

questions.q: A request body contains a __proto__ key. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse creates an own property named __proto__. Object.assign copies it with an assignment, which sets the prototype, so isAdmin appears through inheritance. Spread defines a plain own property instead. This is why fuzz and security tests include keys like __proto__, and why parsers copy only allowed keys.
options: true true
true undefined
undefined undefined
undefined true

questions.q: Rows are rolled back after each "test". What does this print?
questions.explain: The rollback removes the row, so each test sees exactly one. But the sequence behind serial is not transactional: it moved on to 2. Do not assert on generated ids in rollback-isolated tests.
options:
first test id 1 rows 1
second test id 1 rows 1

first test id 1 rows 1
second test id 2 rows 1

first test id 1 rows 1
second test id 2 rows 2

first test id 1 rows 0
second test id 2 rows 0

questions.q: A contract suite runs against a sloppy fake. What does this print?
questions.explain: This fake gets the unit and the test card right, but ignores the reference, so a retry creates a second charge. The real provider would return the first charge. In production that difference means double-charging a customer after a timeout.
options:
PASS amount in kobo
PASS declines tok_declined
PASS idempotent

PASS amount in kobo
PASS declines tok_declined
FAIL idempotent

FAIL amount in kobo
PASS declines tok_declined
FAIL idempotent

PASS amount in kobo
FAIL declines tok_declined
FAIL idempotent

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 12 of 200 requests failed with a 5xx status: 6%. A threshold like k6's http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] fails the run, however fast the successful requests were.
options: 200 6.0% threshold passed
200 6.0% threshold failed
188 6.4% threshold failed
200 4.5% threshold failed

questions.q: Write a stub gateway, declining, whose charge always returns { status: "declined", reason: "insufficient funds" }, and use it so the program prints the declined result.
questions.explain: A stub's job is a canned answer that drives the code down one path. Typing it as PaymentGateway keeps it honest to the interface.

questions.q: Write makeSpy(): it returns a send(to, subject) function that records every call in send.calls as [to, subject]. The program should print the call count and the first call.
questions.explain: That is all a spy is: a function that remembers how it was called. mock.fn() in node:test and vi.fn() in Vitest do the same with more conveniences.

questions.q: Write the builder aLine(overrides): defaults sku "RICE-5KG", unitKobo 950000, quantity 1; any field can be overridden; every call returns a new object.
questions.explain: Spreading the defaults and then the overrides into a new object gives each test its own fixture, with only the interesting fields changed.

questions.q: Write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank method: sort a copy ascending and take the value at position ceil(p / 100 × n) (counting from 1). Do not change the input array.
questions.explain: toSorted returns a sorted copy, so the caller's array keeps its order (latencies[0] is still 120). With ten values, p90 is the 9th smallest and p95 rounds up to the 10th, the single slow request.

questions.q: A small hand-made property check runs total on 1,000 generated carts and vouchers and reports the first negative total. Fix total so the voucher can never take more than the subtotal, and the check prints property holds.
questions.explain: Capping the discount at the subtotal makes the total at least 0 for every input. The loop is a tiny version of what fast-check does, without shrinking; a fixed seed makes it repeatable.

questions.q: Write the fake gateway's charge so it passes the whole contract: amounts stay in kobo, tok_declined is declined, and a repeated reference returns the first result instead of a new charge.
questions.explain: The map by reference is what makes retries safe: the second call finds the first result. A fake that passes the same checks as the real provider is one you can trust in hundreds of other tests.
questions.expected:
PASS amount in kobo
PASS declines tok_declined
PASS idempotent

questions.q: The two "tests" share one store, so their result depends on order. Change them so each test creates its own store with makeStore(). Both orders should then print true true.
questions.explain: With a fresh store per test, no test can see what another one did, so any order gives the same results. In node:test you would create the store in beforeEach.

questions.q: Rewrite priceOf so only real catalog entries have a price: "toString" and "__proto__" must give undefined.
questions.explain: A Map holds only what you put in it. Keeping the object and checking Object.hasOwn(CATALOG, sku) first also works.
questions.expected:
RICE-5KG number
toString undefined
__proto__ undefined
BEANS undefined
